Gravity.discoveryDefinition: Everything with mass attracts something else
Gravity.discoveryExplanation: Gravity is the attraction between objects with mass. They do not need to touch: it acts across distances, and each body attracts the other.
Gravity.discoveryPhenomena: It makes objects fall, keeps the Moon and planets in their orbits and contributes to the tides.
Gravity.discoveryDiagramTitle: Earth and the Moon attract each other
Gravity.discoveryDiagramDescription: Earth and the Moon attract each other with forces of equal magnitude in opposite directions. Sizes and distances are not to scale.
Gravity.discoveryDiagramScale: Conceptual diagram: sizes and distances are not to scale.
Gravity.discoveryHistoryTitle: A history of observation and experiments
Gravity.discoveryHistoryGalileo: He studied how bodies fall and how their motion changes, helping to replace earlier ideas with observations and experiments.
Gravity.discoveryHistoryKepler: He described planetary orbits through three laws, drawing on Tycho Brahe’s astronomical observations.
Gravity.discoveryHistoryNewton: In the Principia, he formulated the law of universal gravitation. Building on earlier work, he used the same interaction to explain falling bodies and the motion of the Moon and planets.
Gravity.discoveryHistoryConstant: G was determined experimentally later. In 1798, Cavendish measured Earth’s density using the attraction between masses: a fundamental precursor to determining G.
Gravity.scienceLawDescription: Describes the magnitude of the gravitational attraction between two masses.
Gravity.scienceConstantDescription: G relates the masses and distance to the force. It is a physical constant whose value is determined through experiments.
Gravity.scienceConstantSpoken: G equals {value} times ten to the power of {exponent}, in newton square metres per square kilogram.

Gravity.everydayTitle: You already know gravity, even without its formula.
Gravity.everydayDescription: The same law connects everyday situations with what happens in space. Start with these three examples.
Gravity.everyday_fall_description: When you let go, Earth pulls the key towards its centre. The key also pulls on Earth, although its effect on Earth is imperceptible.
Gravity.everyday_moon_description: The Moon keeps moving forwards while gravity curves its path around Earth. There is gravity in orbit too.
Gravity.everyday_objects_description: They also attract each other because they have mass. That attraction is very weak: friction with the table keeps them from moving together.

ThreeBody.title: The Three-Body Problem
ThreeBody.description: Discover six orbits and the initial conditions of different solutions to the three-body problem.

what.title: Predicting the motion of three masses
what.description: Given their masses and initial positions and velocities, we seek the motion of three bodies that attract one another solely through gravity.
what.twoDescription: Their relative motion can be solved using conic orbits: ellipses, parabolas or hyperbolas.
what.threeDescription: Each body responds to the other two. Their motions are coupled and can be far more complex.
what.note: The gallery shows six special periodic solutions, rather than every possible kind of motion.

how.title: Three interactions, one system
how.description: The same Newtonian law acts between every pair. There is generally no fixed centre: all three bodies can move.
how.attract: Each pair attracts with forces equal in magnitude and opposite in direction.
how.combine: The vector sum of the other two forces determines each body’s acceleration.
how.evolve: As positions change, distances and forces change. We integrate the equations step by step.
how.note: Masses and initial positions and velocities matter: changing any of them can produce a different evolution.

difficulty.title: A simple law need not produce a simple orbit
difficulty.description: In general, the system cannot be reduced to two-body conic orbits. Its evolution requires studying the coupled interactions.
difficulty.chaos: In some regimes, tiny initial differences grow over time. The laws are deterministic, but long-term predictions are sensitive to the initial precision.
difficulty.periodic: With special initial conditions, positions and velocities repeat after a period. Lagrange and the figure eight are examples.
difficulty.note: Not all three-body systems are chaotic. A periodic orbit need not be stable against perturbations.

history.title: A problem that transformed mechanics
history.newton: Universal gravitation unified attraction between masses. The Moon’s motion under the influence of Earth and the Sun posed the three-body problem.
history.lagrange: He found a family of solutions in which the three bodies keep an equilateral triangle configuration. The gallery shows the circular case.
history.poincare: He revealed the complexity of trajectories and highlighted periodic solutions. His work laid foundations for the study of deterministic chaos.
history.note: Today, numerical simulations let us explore particular solutions; they do not turn the general problem into a single universal orbit.

science.title: Scientific foundations
science.diagramTitle: Three masses and their gravitational interactions
science.diagramDescription: Static diagram, not to scale: three masses connected by three pairs of attractive forces. In each pair, the forces are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction. The lines show separations, not trajectories.
science.diagramCaption: Equal and opposite forces in pairs. Static diagram, not to scale.
science.lawSpoken: Force between bodies i and j equals G times mass i times mass j, divided by the square of their separation.
science.lawDescription: For each pair, attraction grows with mass and decreases with the square of their separation.
science.normalizedTitle: All six solutions: equal masses and G = 1
science.normalized: We use normalized units. Gallery values are not expressed in kg, m or N.
science.periodic: In a periodic solution, positions and velocities repeat after a period T.

detail.idealBodies: These are ideal point masses: the visible dots do not represent their actual physical size.
detail.conditionsDescription: The initial positions and velocities of the three bodies determine how this orbit evolves.
detail.coordinatesHelp: x and y are positions; vₓ and vᵧ are velocities. All values are expressed in normalized units.
detail.refinedConditions: Published seed with local numerical refinement of velocities and period. Published T: {publishedPeriod}. The published parameters and their adjustments are included in the gallery data.
detail.dimensionlessNote: The model is dimensionless: these values must not be interpreted directly as kilograms, metres or seconds.

galleryScience.title: Scientific note
galleryScience.description: These are not decorative curves. Each trajectory is calculated by integrating Newton’s equations with documented initial conditions.
galleryScience.note: The six solutions are compared using a dimensionless system. That is why kg, m and N are not used here as they are in the gravity section.

galleryGuide.title: What do these orbits represent?
galleryGuide.intro: Three bodies attract one another through gravity. Depending on <highlight>where they start and how they move</highlight>, they can follow very different paths.
galleryGuide.keyMessage: The six orbits <highlight>do not occur under arbitrary conditions</highlight>. Our simulations use <highlight>equal masses (1), G = 1, and specific initial positions and velocities</highlight> to reproduce each solution.
galleryGuide.diagramDescription: Diagram of three bodies attracting one another through gravity, showing the distances between them and their initial velocities.
galleryGuide.diagramCaption: The lines show the distances between the bodies. The green arrows show their initial velocities. This is a visual example, not one of the six orbits.
galleryGuide.modelDescription: We simulate three bodies attracting one another through gravity. We use equal masses and two-dimensional motion to study their trajectories.
galleryGuide.equationDescription: Gravitational attraction depends on the masses of the bodies and the distance between them.
galleryGuide.massDescription: All three bodies have the same mass. In our simulations, each mass equals 1.
galleryGuide.positionDescription: These determine where each body starts. Every orbit requires specific starting positions.
galleryGuide.velocityDescription: These determine how fast and in which direction each body starts moving. Every orbit requires specific values.
galleryGuide.distanceDescription: These show how far apart the bodies are. The distances change as the bodies move and affect gravitational attraction.
galleryGuide.periodDescription: The time required for a periodic orbit to complete one cycle and return approximately to its initial state.
galleryGuide.integrationDescription: The computer calculates the bodies' positions and velocities step by step using Newton's equations and a numerical method called adaptive RK4.
galleryGuide.importantTitle: Why are the six orbits different?
galleryGuide.importantDescription: All six use equal masses and G = 1, but they do not all start in the same way. Lagrange begins as an equilateral triangle. The other five start with aligned bodies and different initial positions or velocities. Each combination reproduces a known periodic solution.
galleryGuide.modelNote: These six simulations use equal masses, G = 1 and two-dimensional motion. These are features of the model we use, not requirements for every three-body problem.
galleryGuide.shapeNote: <highlight>Lagrange</highlight> starts as a triangle. <highlight>The other five orbits</highlight> start with aligned bodies, but use different initial conditions.
galleryGuide.takeaway: To reproduce each of these six orbits, we need <highlight>its specific initial conditions</highlight>. Changing those values can change the motion and prevent it from repeating. <highlight>There is no single minimum distance or speed</highlight> that guarantees all six solutions.

hints.units: Check units first: 1 km = 1000 m, 1 cm = 0.01 m and 1 t = 1000 kg.
hints.conversion: Consider whether the target unit is larger or smaller and which conversion factor connects them.
hints.square: Squaring means multiplying a quantity by itself.
hints.denominator: r² is in the denominator. First consider how that square changes.
hints.formula: F = G · m₁ · m₂ / r². Convert to kg and m before substituting.
hints.exponent: A negative exponent means dividing by a power of ten.
hints.decimal: Move the decimal point and count the places to get a coefficient between 1 and 10.
hints.mass: Look at the mass in the numerator and what stays constant.
hints.mutual: Think of Newton’s third law: action and reaction.
hints.attraction: Gravity is an interaction between bodies with mass.
